If the cell is not transparent, sample the source data within that block and perform standard front-to-back compositing [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that if a cell is not transparent, one should sample the source data within that block and perform standard front-to-back compositing. The evidence in Source [S2] describes an acceleration structure where each cell corresponds to a 32x32x32 block in the source data, containing min/max values to determine transparency. The text explicitly states that if the space is transparent, it 'may be skipped by a ray.' By logical inference, if the space is not transparent (i.e., it contains data), the ray must proceed to sample that block. Standard volume rendering (DVR) involves front-to-back compositing. Therefore, the claim accurately reflects the procedure implied by the evidence: skip if transparent, otherwise process (sample and composite) the block.
